title: Bechukotai: if ye walk (Leviticus 26:3)
hookLine: the blessings begin with walking in God's ways
tomorrow: Bechukotai: I will walk among you (Leviticus 26:12)

cards: Jewish law, in Hebrew, is halachah. You'd guess it means rules, or code. It comes from the verb to walk, halach.
The walk. The going. Not a building you live inside, not a wall you stay behind.

A road. Today's portion, the last in Leviticus, opens its long list of blessings with that same verb. Before the rain, before the harvest, before peace, comes a single condition, and it's a way of moving.

teach.h: IF YE WALK IN MY STATUTES.
teach.b: Leviticus twenty-six, verse three: "If ye walk in My statutes, and keep My commandments, and do them". The portion takes its name from that verse: Bechukotai, in My statutes. What follows is a cascade.
Rain in its season. Trees heavy with fruit. Threshing that runs until the grape harvest, and grape harvest until sowing, so the work of the year never quite catches up with the plenty.
Peace in the land. You'll lie down, and none shall make you afraid. But the commentators stopped at the first line.
The Sifra, the ancient rabbinic reading of Leviticus, asks: keep My commandments and do them is already in the verse, so what does if ye walk in My statutes add?
Its answer, which Rashi repeats: toiling in Torah. Learning that costs some effort, the way a long walk costs some breath. Another strand of reading hears something else in the verb.
You don't walk in a place once. A walk is daily, repeated, step after step, the ordinary distance between your door and the bus. Blessing, in this reading, isn't promised to a single heroic moment.
It's attached to a pace. Some readers link the word for statutes, chukim, to a root that means to engrave, to cut into stone. Read that way, the line holds a tension.
The fixed thing becomes a path.

how: Bechukotai is the last portion of Leviticus, read in the spring and often paired with Behar. The idea that Jewish law is a halachah, a way of walking, runs through Jewish teaching about daily practice.

games.q: the verse already says "keep My commandments, and do them." so what does "walk in My statutes" add, according to the Sifra?
o: toiling in Torah: learning that takes effort.
games.why: the Sifra, and Rashi after it, read walking as working at Torah study. the extra phrase must teach something new.

practice: If you can, stand and walk slowly, even just across a room and back; if you can't, let your feet press the floor in turn, left, right, left.
With each step, ask one quiet question: where are my daily steps actually pointing this year? Not where I'm supposed to be, but where I'm headed.
